_meta.scope: Curated, verified ways to support Cherokee and Indigenous lives today — directly from Cherokee-led and Indigenous-led organizations wherever possible.
_meta.policy: Donations flow directly to the organizations, not through this app. No affiliate links. No revenue sharing. Nothing is tracked or intermediated. These are civic-minded links to publicly-operated Cherokee and Indigenous institutions.
_meta.opener: The Cherokee Nation, the Eastern Band of Cherokee Indians, and the United Keetoowah Band are sovereign nations that exist right now. If this project matters to you, the most meaningful response is not to remember the past — it is to support the living present.

categories.label: Donate
categories.intro: Direct financial support to Cherokee-led and Indigenous-led organizations. All are 501(c)(3) nonprofits.

actions.title: Cherokee Nation Foundation
actions.description: Awarded more than $500,000 in scholarships for the 2025–2026 academic year, including language-fluency incentives. Supports Cherokee youth pursuing higher education.

actions.title: Cherokee Preservation Foundation
actions.tagline: EBCI language, culture, and community programs
actions.description: Funds the Kituwah Preservation & Education Program, New Kituwah Academy immersion school, and cultural preservation across the Qualla Boundary. Primary funder of EBCI language revitalization work.

actions.title: Kituwah Preservation & Education Program (KPEP)
actions.tagline: Direct support to EBCI language preservation
actions.description: The EBCI's in-house language program. Runs the Cherokee Speaker Archive Project, New Kituwah Academy curriculum, and cultural translation services. Contact info@ebcikpep.com for partnership.

actions.title: Native American Rights Fund (NARF)
actions.tagline: Legal defense of Native rights and treaties
actions.description: Founded 1970; 4-star Charity Navigator rating. Fights in U.S. courts for tribal sovereignty, treaty rights, and Native representation. Represented the Cherokee Nation in reservation-affirmation cases post-McGirt.

actions.title: First Nations Development Institute
actions.description: Grants to Native-led nonprofits across Indian Country for food sovereignty, youth development, entrepreneurship, and language. Cherokee Nation and EBCI have been grantees.

categories.label: Learn
categories.intro: Free and low-cost resources to deepen your own knowledge — directly from Cherokee sources.

actions.title: Cherokee Nation Dictionary App
actions.description: Over 6,000 Cherokee words with native-speaker audio, syllabary, phonetics, grammar notes, and biographical info on first-language speakers. Built by the Cherokee Nation Language Department.

actions.title: Cherokee on Memrise
actions.description: Free Cherokee language curriculum built in partnership with the Cherokee Nation Language Department. Video clips of spoken dialects included.

actions.title: Cherokee Phoenix
actions.description: Founded by Elias Boudinot at New Echota; the oldest Native American newspaper. Suppressed in 1835, revived in 1977, still publishing. Subscribe or read free online.

actions.title: The One Feather (EBCI)
actions.description: EBCI's independent newspaper covering Qualla Boundary life, tribal politics, and cultural events. Covered the 2026 Nikwasi Mound deed return ceremony.

actions.title: Indian Country Today (ICT)
actions.description: Pan-tribal journalism covering Native America — sovereignty, federal policy, culture, and contemporary Indigenous voices. Listened widely in Indian Country.

actions.title: Reading list — Cherokee-authored
actions.description: Daniel Heath Justice (Cherokee Nation), Our Fire Survives the Storm • Julie L. Reed (Cherokee Nation), Serving the Nation • Wilma Mankiller, A Chief and Her People • Robert J. Conley (UKB), The Cherokee Nation: A History.

categories.label: Visit
categories.intro: Walk the places Cherokee people lived, died, resisted, and built. Admission fees support tribal and state preservation work.

actions.title: Museum of the Cherokee People
actions.description: Founded 1948 — one of the oldest continually-operating tribal museums in the United States. Located on the Qualla Boundary, the ancestral homeland of all Cherokees.

actions.title: Kituwah Mound
actions.tagline: Bryson City, NC · The Mother Town
actions.description: 5,000-year-old Cherokee platform mound; the spiritual center of the Cherokee people. Returned to EBCI ownership in 1996 after 200+ years. Free to visit during daylight hours.

actions.title: Nikwasi (Noquisiyi) Mound
actions.description: 1,000-year-old platform mound; home of the Nunnehi. Deed transferred to EBCI on February 26, 2026, the first Indigenous mound formally returned to tribal ownership in North Carolina.

actions.title: New Echota State Historic Site
actions.description: The Cherokee capital where the 1827 Constitution was ratified, the Phoenix was first printed, and General Scott arrived with 7,000 troops in May 1838. Reconstructed council house on the original foundation.

actions.title: Red Clay State Historic Park
actions.tagline: Cleveland, TN · The last Cherokee capital in the East
actions.description: Where the Cherokee Nation continued to meet in council after Georgia extended state laws over Cherokee territory (1832–1838). "Camp Ross" — the final capital before removal.

actions.title: Trail of Tears National Historic Trail
actions.description: The National Park Service's certified multi-state trail network across nine states — Blythe Ferry, Mantle Rock, Trail of Tears State Park (MO), Fort Smith. Certified sites are open to the public with interpretive markers.
actions.cta: Find a site near you · nps.gov/trte

actions.title: Cherokee Heritage Center
actions.tagline: Tahlequah, OK · Cherokee Nation cultural center
actions.description: Cherokee National Historical Society's heritage center in the Cherokee Nation capital. Includes the Trail of Tears Exhibit, Cherokee Family Research Center, and archival Cherokee newspapers.

categories.label: Acknowledge
categories.intro: Whatever your ZIP code, Indigenous nations lived there before you. Learn whose land you are on.

actions.title: Native Land Digital map
actions.tagline: Type any place. See whose land it is.
actions.description: Interactive map by Native Land Digital — an Indigenous-led nonprofit mapping Indigenous territories, languages, and treaties across the Americas, Australia, and more. Enter any address to see which nation(s) historically occupied that land.

actions.title: Cherokee historical territory
actions.description: See the ancestral 40,000-square-mile Cherokee homeland across modern Tennessee, North Carolina, Georgia, Alabama, South Carolina, Virginia, West Virginia, and Kentucky.

actions.title: Cherokee Nation citizenship (for eligible descendants)
actions.tagline: Lineal descent from the Dawes Roll
actions.description: If you believe you descend from a Cherokee ancestor on the Dawes Roll (1898–1914), the Cherokee Nation Registration Office can guide you through documentation and enrollment. No blood quantum required.

categories.label: Advocate
categories.intro: Cherokee sovereignty, Indigenous rights, and federal recognition are live policy fights. These Indigenous-led organizations drive them.

actions.title: IllumiNative
actions.description: Founded by Crystal Echo Hawk. Fights Native invisibility in media, education, and policy; runs research on contemporary perceptions of Native peoples and supports Indigenous-led narrative work.

actions.title: National Congress of American Indians (NCAI)
actions.tagline: Oldest, largest American Indian & Alaska Native advocacy org
actions.description: Founded 1944. Represents tribal governments and communities before Congress, the White House, and the courts. Cherokee Nation is a long-time member.
